text: I present a study of deep learning (DL) approaches for docking small molecules into protein receptors.
This is a mainstay computational problem in structure-based drug discovery, but surprisingly, recent advances in DL techniques have not yet achieved their projected potential for docking.

This chapter introduces structure-based drug discovery (Section 1.1), docking (Section 1.2), and DL (Section 1.3), as well as the motivation for this work (Section 1.4) and the structure of the thesis (Section 1.5).

Structure-based drug discovery is a paradigm for developing molecules, which when small are often called “ligands”, that bind to other molecules, which are called “targets” or “receptors”, using knowledge of the three-dimensional structures of both molecules.
The central idea is that binding requires the ligand’s shape and chemical features to be complementary to the receptor.

Whether the resulting binding event produces the intended therapeutic effect that makes this compound a drug candidate is determined by the biological target involved, the binding site of the ligand, and the strength of their interaction, in addition to a range of pharmacological constraints (Patrick, 2023, ch.
The ligand’s target specificity, in turn, influences its potential to cause side effects.
Understanding the structural characteristics of target molecules and how to design ligands with complementary features unique to a selected target is a cornerstone of rational drug discovery.
Structure-based drug discovery is only possible because we know the structures of many biomolecules.

Thanks to the continuous improvement of the experimental techniques X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and cryogenic electron microscopy over the past 80 years, we have the structures of increasingly large and biologically important molecules—from small compounds such as penicillin (Crowfoot et al., 1949, 17 atoms) to peptides such as insulin (M. J. Adams et al., 1969, 788 atoms) and even large proteins such as the 2019-nCoV S protein (Wrapp et al., 2020, 4634 atoms).

Access to these structures has led to breakthroughs in drug discovery and production, elucidation of the mechanisms of action, and the very field of rational drug design (Hägg & Crowfoot Hodgkin, 1999).

Small molecules, namely organic molecules with up to 100 atoms, which can be administered orally, are a very important and the most used drug modality, and proteins are the most common targets (Ritter, 2024).
Newer drug modalities such as macrocycles, peptides, or antibodies (Valeur et al., 2017) and other targets such as RNA and DNA provide other avenues for drug discovery.
For my thesis I focus on small molecule drugs that target proteins.

Currently, the two most important repositories of experimentally determined structures for proteins and small molecules are the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al., 2000) and the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) (F. H. Allen et al., 1991) respectively.

The PDB serves as a de facto legal deposit library for protein structures, since most journals require authors to submit structural data upon publication, making it the largest source of protein and protein-complex structures.

The CSD similarly aggregates crystal structures from researchers worldwide, with a strong emphasis on crystallographic data, and contains nearly all known drugs as well as a wide range of drug-like molecules.
In December 2025, the PDB and the CSD contained 246 715 and 1 376 589 unique, experimentally resolved structures, respectively.1 A drug must be produced, stored, and administered.
It must reach its target in a patient and provide a therapeutic benefit with minimal side-effects (Young, 2009, ch.

Because other important properties of drugs have been directly linked to the structures of small molecules, structure-based drug discovery has become a multi-objective optimisation in which favourable interactions are only one criterion.

Examples of computational proxies that link structure to pharmacological properties are estimates of physicochemical parameters such as prediction of log 𝑃 as an estimate of lipophilicity (Wildman & Crippen, 1999), Lipinski’s ‘rule of 5’ for oral administration effectiveness (Lipinski et al., 1997), and drug-likeness scores (Bickerton et al., 2012).
As we shall see in the next section, docking methods are designed to model molecular interactions and do not help optimise pharmacological properties beyond binding (Young, 2009, ch.
Beyond biological properties, there are other chemical and legal limitations that affect drug design.

Our current chemical knowledge limits which molecules can be synthesised and tested, often delineated by synthetic accessibility estimators (Ertl & Schuffenhauer, 2009), supplier catalogues, synthesis planning tools (Segler et al., 2018), and expert chemists.
Patents further limit the design space of small molecules, as one would sensibly exclude all structures patented by others.

Docking is a computational approach to predict the binding mode of a ligand when bound to a receptor.
Docking algorithms require as input a 3D structure of the receptor, a description of the ligand, and a search space.
Given these inputs, docking algorithms generate as output the 3D structure of the receptor-ligand binding complex (Figure 1.1).
The first input, the 3D receptor structure, should be as close as possible to the holo (ligand-bound) form of the protein.
Using the apo (unbound) form may be appropriate when the structural differences between the apo and holo states are small.

For highly flexible proteins in which the side chains or the backbone undergo conformational changes upon ligand binding, the holo form of the receptor bound to a related ligand may be a more suitable starting point.
In practice, PDB structures are often used, but care must be taken to prepare them, for example by selecting plausible protonation states of the side chains in the binding site (Bender et al., 2021).
In certain cases, the use of multiple receptor structures is advantageous, and the use of snapshots generated from molecular dynamics simulations has been demonstrated (Dunn et al., 2024).
The second input, the ligand molecule, is typically provided with a 3D starting conformation.

Ideally, an unbiased conformation of a ligand is used, one that has not undergone, for example, the minimisation procedure used to generate experimental protein-ligand structures, which would affect the ligand’s bond lengths, angles, and rings.
The PDB provides idealised versions of ligand structures as part of the Chemical Component Dictionary (Westbrook et al., 2015).

Some docking software allow as input 1D string representations (see Appendix A, Section A.1.1) because the software includes a conformation generation module that can generate or regenerate 3D coordinates.

Most docking software requires the user to carefully prepare the ligand by defining the stereochemistry, charges, protonation, and tautomeric state; these are all properties that are typically modelled as fixed during docking (Torres et al., 2019).
The third input, the search space restricts the set of solutions that a docking algorithm can output.
Typically, ligand placement is restricted to a defined region of the receptor that encompasses a binding site.
In some cases, the search space is expanded to include the entire protein to perform blind docking.
The search space may be reduced by positional constraints on specific ligand substructures and enlarged by allowing some movement of protein side chains.
Most targets do not undergo large conformational changes and modelling only side-chain flexibility is sufficient (J. J. Clark et al., 2019).
The two primary outputs of docking methods are the predicted ligand coordinates and an associated docking score.

In principle, a single predicted pose may correspond to any of the many microstates between which a ligand binding mode fluctuates; in practice, however, docking results are typically evaluated by comparison with experimentally determined structures (Paggi et al., 2024).
Most docking tools, therefore, report a set of ligand poses paired with corresponding scores.
These scores are used by docking programmes to rank poses of the same ligand and externally by users to prioritise a variety of molecular candidates.
Some methods report scores in the units of binding affinity (kcal/mol); for example, AutoDock Vina (Trott & Olson, 2010).

However, docking-derived affinity estimates are generally considered too inaccurate to reliably predict true binding affinities (Pantsar & Poso, 2018), although improving their accuracy remains an active area of research (G. Durant et al., 2025).
In this thesis, I focus on pose generation.
The main applications of docking are the discovery of potentially new ligands, the optimisation of lead compounds, and the investigation of the mode of action (Paggi et al., 2024).

Lead discovery by virtual screening with docking proceeds by predicting the binding poses of a (large) set of molecules from a library, measuring the best fit of each molecule, and then ranking the candidates and selecting the top ones as leads.

In ligand optimisation, medicinal chemists inspect lead compounds and their fit with the receptor in order to propose modifications to the molecular structure with the goal of optimising the binding strength or other molecular properties, often iteratively.
For target function analysis, ligands known to elicit biological responses are docked and the differences in the target structure are analysed.
One specialised application of docking explored later in this thesis is the use of docking with constraints in fragment-based drug discovery.

Fragments, ligands with a molecular mass of less than 300 Da, can be used to explore the binding site of a protein effectively, and can be combined into regular sized ligands by growing, linking, and merging (AlKharboush et al., 2025).
Docking with substructure constraints derived from fragments can assist in designing ligand elaborations by helping to determine the fit of the added substructures.

Other more specialised applications of docking related to structure-based drug discovery include fitting ligands to electron densities (Roseman, 2000), uncovering reaction mechanisms of enzymes (Das et al., 2019), and studying host-guest systems (Casbarra & Procacci, 2021).

Dedicated software packages, for example PHENIX (P. D. Adams et al., 2010), which provide pipelines for experimental structure solution, include docking routines to place substructures of the model onto electron maps (Liebschner et al., 2019).
Improvements in docking algorithms therefore impact many aspects of structural biology, and not just drug discovery directly.
The three main requirements for docking algorithms are speed, accuracy, and generalisability.

Speed is needed because virtual screening libraries can be very large, with up to a billion molecules for ‘ultra-large screens’ (Gorgulla et al., 2020); the requirement for speed is further exacerbated by the need to consider multiple structural snapshots of the target when docking into a rigid receptor.
Accuracy in terms of recovering the true binding mode is important for decision making in drug discovery (Warren et al., 2006) and to avoid taking “duds” further down the drug discovery pipeline.
Generalisation to new protein targets and new ligands is a must because docking for drug discovery, by definition, must predict unknown protein-ligand interactions.
Classical docking algorithms typically break the problem of predicting binding modes into two subroutines: sampling and scoring (Young, 2009, ch.
The sampling subroutine generates co- ordinates for the ligand atoms, and the scoring subroutine grades these coordinates.
Often there is a feedback loop from the scoring to the sampling routine.
In the last 43 years, more than 100 docking methods have been developed (Pagadala et al., 2017), and some examples are listed in Table 1.1.

The large number of docking methods reflect the diversity of computational approaches that have been applied to the docking problem: Monte Carlo simulated annealing is a stochastic method from physics that is used for docking in the AutoDock series (Goodsell & Olson, 1990; Morris et al., 1998, 2009; Trott & Olson, 2010).
Genetic algorithms are stochastic search algorithms that are used in GOLD (Jones et al., 1997) and AutoDock 2 (Morris et al., 1998).
Fragment- based incremental construction builds solutions step-wise starting from small fragments and is used in HOOK (Eisen et al., 1994), FlexX (Rarey et al., 1996), and SEED (Majeux et al., 1999).

Systematic search approaches exhaustively enumerate poses by discretising the search space and are used by Hammerhead (Welch et al., 1996), EUDOC (Pang et al., 2001), and in combination with pruning also by Glide (Friesner et al., 2004).
The diversity of published approaches highlights the amount of algorithmic experimentation done and the maturity of classical docking methods.
Despite the large number of docking approaches, docking as a paradigm remains limited in some important ways.
Being structure-based, the methods require a receptor structure as input.
Rigid docking, that is assuming a rigid receptor structure, is the most common and most reliable approach.
Flexible docking, allowing some movement of the receptor, is slow and often does not perform better than rigid docking (Paggi et al., 2024).

Further limitations are that the protonation and charge patterns of the ligand and receptor are fixed during the docking (Petukh et al., 2013) and water molecules are only selectively modelled (Forli & Olson, 2012).
Despite these limitations, docking has been and remains an important tool in structure-based drug design.
Possible improvements of docking methods are faster predictions, better control, and richer models.

The first, faster predictions, is for docking ligands into flexible receptors which currently often requires some use of molecular dynamics or docking to a variety of crystal structures of the same target.
The second, better control, is the methods’ flexibility for users to test hypotheses, around, for example, the binding site, substructure positions, and desired interactions (e.g. H-bond, covalent).
The last category, richer models, includes improved modelling of waters, receptor flexibility, charges, protonation, and tautomeric states.
These factors are known to be important in protein-ligand binding and docking programs should more accurately model them.
Deep learning (DL) is a subfield of machine learning.
Machine learning is an approach to build functions, called models, that do not require a programmer to implement all rules by hand.
Rather, the programmer defines parameters that are left to be inferred from data in a process called “training”.
Once the parameters have been determined by training, the model can be used like a regular function.
Supervised learning is one approach to train a machine learning model.
Given pairs of input and desired output, the model is trained to reproduce these data (see Appendix A, Section A.2.1).

The goal is to find parameters that both reproduce the training data and lead to sensible outputs for new, previously unseen inputs that were not shown during training, so that the model can be used to make predictions.
If a model can make satisfactory predictions on new data points, it generalises; a model that does not generalise is said to be overfitting to its training data (Goodfellow et al., 2016, ch.
To assess generalisation when building a model, machine learning engineers split the example data into a training set and a test set.
The training set is used to find the parameters of the model and the test set is used to assess the generalisability of the model.

If there are modelling decisions that cannot be made by the programmer or the model has parameters that cannot be learnt, so-called “hyper-parameters”, then a third split, the validation set, is used to select these To quantify the agreement between a predicted output and ground truth data, a loss function must be specified for supervised training.
Given a data point and the model’s prediction, it returns a positive real number, the loss.
A loss of 0 means that the two data points (actual and predicted) are identical.
The definition of a loss function is an important consideration in supervised machine learning; an underspecified loss function can lead to surprising failure modes of the model.
Often, loss functions combine multiple objectives; for example, by adding different loss components linearly to obtain one main loss.
The loss function is essential because it defines what constitutes good performance on a task.
DL is the sub-set of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with a large number of hidden layers to learn patterns directly from data.
These models typically have a large number of parameters (see Appendix A, Section A.2.2).

DL typically does not rely on human-chosen data representations but uses raw representations of the input to directly learn patterns from the data, including intermediate representations at every layer (Goodfellow et al., 2016, ch.
Neural networks are trained by making small adjustments to the parameters iteratively.
A typical training algorithm involves setting the initial parameter values according to a random initialisation scheme, for example, Xavier initialisation (Glorot & Bengio, 2010).
Then batches of the data (inputs and outputs) are drawn from the training set.
The model makes predictions on the inputs, and these predictions are compared to the ground truth outputs using the loss function.
The back-propagation algorithm (Rojas, 1996), using the chain rule of calculus, is then used to calculate how much each parameter affects the loss function.
These derivatives are then used to update the parameters, using, for example, gradient descent (Bishop & Bishop, 2024, ch.
7) or more sophisticated stochastic optimisation methods such as Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014).
This procedure is repeated by passing over all the training data multiple times; one pass is called an “epoch”.
Neural networks are highly flexible and, in principle, can approximate any function with enough neurones and hidden layers (Funahashi, 1989; Hornik et al., 1989).
This is particularly useful for non- tabular data for which few other universal modelling approaches exist.
However, this universality does not mean that DL models can be used to solve any problem.

Indeed, no learning algorithm is, in general, the best, when considering all possible problems (Wolpert, 1996); what makes neural networks so useful is that they contain important inductive biases, for example smoothness, that are useful for a large set of relevant problems (Bishop & Bishop, 2024, ch.
In practice, it is possible to include other problem-specific inductive biases such as translation invariance or permutation equivariance, and that makes DL so useful.
However, the main downside of DL models is that they require large amounts of training data to learn from.
In many domains, including structural biology, the input data have an intrinsic structure.
For example, proteins consist of a small set of identical amino acids connected in sequence, forming chains that mostly fold up in repeating patterns.

Understanding the internal structure of the data, the necessary degrees of freedom of a task, and task-specific mathematics have led to new inductive biases, e.g. triangle inequality inspired triangular updates (Jumper et al., 2021), which have led to breakthroughs.
Choosing a DL framework that follows the structure of the data generating process constitutes an inductive bias that helps a model learn a task more efficiently and using fewer data.
Other examples of common network architectures with strong inductive biases that we will encounter later include convolutional networks, graph neural networks, and diffusion models.
Section A.2 provides technical background on these and other DL–based models that have been applied to docking.
A particularly successful DL model architecture is the transformer (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017).
It is suitable for all types of data, for example sequential data in conjunction with positional encodings (see Appendix A, Section A.2.6).
The transformer has become a universal building block, and many tasks that were solved with more dedicated architectures have now been solved with transformers.
The two main advantages of transformers are that they are well suited for parallel processing and that they are effective at transfer learning.

This has led some researchers to state that, like search, DL represents a paradigm shift and that training (a transformer) with sufficient data is sufficient to build a supervised model for any task, and even reach artificial general intelligence (Bishop & Bishop, 2024, ch.
Whether this is true or not is not yet known.
I can only note that DL-based modelling is still relatively young in comparison to purely mathematical or physics-based modelling.
Deep learning (DL) techniques have led to major breakthroughs in protein structure prediction, recognised by the award of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Nobel Foundation, 2024).
John Jumper and Demis Hassabis were honoured for developing AlphaFold 2 (Jumper et al., 2021), a DL-based method capable of generating highly accurate models of protein structures.

AlphaFold 2 won the fourteenth biennial Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction competition (CASP14) in 2020 (Jumper et al., 2021), and two years later, DL-based methods inspired by AlphaFold 2 dominated CASP15, establishing DL as the dominant method in protein structure prediction (Kryshtafovych et al., 2023).
These advances in computational protein structure prediction are significant for structure-based drug discovery because they can provide structures of more potential drug targets.

While the experimentally determined protein structures in the PDB cover about 35 % of the genes of the human genome (Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2021), the computationally generated structures in the AlphaFold Data Base (Varadi et al., 2024) cover more than 98 % of human proteins.

This increase unlocks many new targets, for example the computational structure of glucose-6-phosphatase protein is amenable to structure- based drug discovery and Tunyasuvunakool et al. (2021) speculate that a ligand that binds to a pocket near the protein’s binding face may help regulate blood sugar levels.
The aforementioned success of DL in protein structure prediction and the implications for structure- based drug discovery motivated me to investigate DL applied in docking.

My guiding hypothesis is that DL-based docking methods are still early on the innovation S-curve (Asthana, 1995), and are less mature than the incumbent methods in functionality and performance, but also that the technology has the potential to replace the incumbent methods.

The first successful application of DL techniques applied to docking that I am aware of is the DL-based scoring function in NNScore (Durrant & Mc- Cammon, 2010) that uses a convolutional neural network and takes as input a voxel grid.
The first approaches that used DL also for pose generation include DeepDock (Méndez-Lucio et al., 2021) that learnt a statistical potential.
Table 1.2 lists twenty DL-based methods, four of which had been published when I started this work in 2022.

The large number of publications of DL-based docking approaches over the following years demonstrates not only the timeliness of my work but also, in general, the field’s belief that DL could have a large impact on docking.
However, none of the approaches published by 2022 had the level of impact on docking that AlphaFold 2 had on protein structure prediction—and this marks the starting point of my thesis.
In Chapter 2, I describe a benchmark of classical and DL-based docking methods to investigate their failure modes and make suggestions for their improvement.

In Chapter 3, I assess the quality of the training and test data sets on which the DL-based docking methods have been trained in an attempt to understand the failure modes of the models relative to the data.
In Chapter 4, I use experimental data to measure to what extent similar ligands adopt similar poses upon binding.

In Chapter 5, I explore diffusion guidance using molecular mechanics force field-inspired terms to fix the observed failure modes of a leading DL-based docking method, and I add further terms to constrain substructures and interactions using the insights I gathered in Chapter 4.
Lastly, Chapter 6 concludes my thesis and introduces the new paradigm of co-folding methods and provides an outlook on DL-based techniques for small molecule docking.
As I discussed in Chapter 1, the last few years have seen the development of numerous deep learning (DL)-based protein-ligand docking methods.
If AlphaFold 2 is any guide, they offer huge promise in terms of speed and accuracy.

However, despite claims of state-of-the-art performance in terms of root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) to experimentally determined poses, upon closer inspection, I found that they often produce physically implausible molecular structures.
It is therefore not sufficient to evaluate these methods solely by RMSD to a crystallographic native binding mode.
It is vital, particularly for DL-based methods, that they are also evaluated in terms of steric and energetic criteria.

I present PoseBusters (Buttenschoen et al., 2024), a Python package that performs a series of standard quality checks, built using the well-established cheminformatics toolkit RDKit (Landrum The PoseBusters test suite validates chemical and geometric consistency of a ligand including its stereochemistry, and the physical plausibility of intra- and intermolecular measurements such as the planarity of aromatic rings, standard bond lengths, and protein-ligand clashes.
Only methods that both pass these stereochemical and energetic checks and predict native-like binding modes should be classed as having “state-of-the-art” performance.

I will show that in terms of both physical plausibility and the ability to generalise to examples that are distinct from the training data, none of the DL-based methods I tested outperformed classical docking tools.
In addition, I will show that molecular mechanics force fields contain docking-relevant physics that appears to be missing from DL methods.

PoseBusters allows practitioners to assess docking and molecular generation methods and will help drive innovation in new inductive biases still required to improve DL-based methods and ultimately the development methods that generate more accurate and more realistic predictions.

As described in Chapter 1, molecular docking, an essential step in structure-based drug discovery (De Ruyck et al., 2016), is the task of predicting the predominant binding mode(s) of a protein-ligand complex given an experimentally solved or computationally modelled protein structure and a ligand structure (Morris & Lim-Wilby, 2008).

The predicted complexes are often used in a virtual screening workflow to help select small molecules from a large library of possible candidates (Lionta et al., 2014); or directly by medicinal chemists to understand the binding mode and to decide whether a small molecule is a suitable drug candidate (Patrick, 2023, ch.
Docking methods are designed with the understanding that binding is enabled by interactions between protein and ligand structures.
But due to the complexity of this, methods tend to strike a balance between fast calculation and accuracy (Patrick, 2023, ch.

DL, as described in Chapter 1, promises to disrupt the dominant design principle of classical docking software, and DL-based docking methods promise to unlock fast and accurate virtual screening for drug discovery.

To this end, several different DL-based docking methods have already been proposed (Corso et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2022; Méndez-Lucio et al., 2021; Stärk et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023); see also Table 1.2 for a more complete list.

Non-DL-based “classical” docking methods include within their search and scoring functions terms that ensure chemical consistency and physical plausibility; for example, limiting the degrees of movement in the ligand to only the rotatable bonds in the ligand and including penalties if the protein and ligand clash (Goodsell & Olson, 1990; Jones et al., 1995; Trott & Olson, 2010).

In this chapter, I show that some current DL-based docking methods still lack such key “inductive biases”, resulting in the creation of unrealistic chemical structures and binding modes despite obtaining root-mean-squared deviation (RMSD) values (see Appendix A, Section A.1.3) from the experimental binding mode that are less than the widely-used 2 Å threshold (Cole et al., 2005).

To assess the output of docking methods, I created an independent test suite called PoseBusters (Buttenschoen et al., 2024) that checks the chemical consistency and physical plausibility alongside established metrics, such as the binding mode RMSD.
The problem of assessing the physical plausibility of docking predictions is akin to the structure validation of ligand data in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al., 2000; Shao et al., 2022).

Structure validation assesses the agreement of each of the ligands’ bond lengths and angles with those observed in related chemical structures and the presence of steric clashes both within the ligand and between it and its surroundings (Shao et al., 2022).

While these tests were designed for users to select those ligand crystal structures which are likely to be correct (Shao et al., 2022), docking methods are evaluated on their ability to recover crystal structures, so their output should pass the same physical plausibility tests.
Physical plausibility checks are also part of some workflows for conformation generation (Friedrich, de Bruyn Kops et al., 2017; Hawkins et al., 2010).

Friedrich, de Bruyn Kops et al. (2017) use geometry checks performed by NAOMI (Urbaczek et al., 2011) which measures—like the PDB tests just mentioned—the deviation from known optimal values for bond lengths and bond angles, and also tests for divergence from planarity for aromatic rings.
In addition to physical checks, chemical checks are also needed (Warren et al., 2012).

Chemical checks proposed for checking PDB structures include the identification of mislabelled stereo assignment, inconsistent bonding patterns, missing functional groups, and unlikely ionisation states (Warren et al., 2012).

The problem of checking chemical plausibility has also come up in de novo molecule generation, where Brown et al. (2019) proposed a test suite including checks for the chemical validity of any proposed molecule.

For docking, the focus is less on stability and synthetic accessibility of a generated molecular structure as it is hoped that these have been tested prior to attempting docking, but more on chemical consistency and physical realism of the predicted bound conformation.

Some comparisons of docking methods have included additional metrics based on volume overlap (Warren et al., 2006) or protein-ligand interactions (Ciancetta et al., 2014) to supplement pose accuracybased metrics such as RMSD of atomic positions and run time measurements, but the majority of comparisons of docking methods are predominantly based on binding mode RMSD (Bolcato et al., 2019; Cole et al., 2005; Onodera et al., 2007; Plewczynski et al., 2011).
The current standard practice of comparing the output conformations of docking methods using on RMSD-based metrics alone also extends to recent new methods.

The five DL-based docking methods that I test in this chapter (Corso et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2022; Méndez-Lucio et al., 2021; Stärk et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023) all claimed better performance than standard docking methods but these claims rested entirely on the sole criterion on RMSD.
None of these methods tested their outputs for physical plausibility.
In this chapter, I present PoseBusters, a test suite that is designed to identify implausible chemical structures, conformations and ligand poses.

I used PoseBusters to evaluate the predicted binding modes generated by the five DL-based docking methods described earlier and listed in Table 2.1 and two standard non-DL-based “classical” docking methods AutoDock Vina (Trott & Olson, 2010) and GOLD (Verdonk et al., 2003).

These poses were generated by re-docking the cognate ligands of the 81 protein- ligand crystal complexes in the Astex Diverse set (Hartshorn et al., 2007) and 308 ligands of the protein- ligand crystal complexes in the PoseBusters Benchmark set, a new set of complexes released from 2021 onwards, into their cognate receptor crystal structures.

On the commonly-used Astex Diverse set, the DL-based docking method DiffDock appears to perform best in terms of RMSD alone but when taking physical plausibility into account, AutoDock Vina and GOLD perform best.

On the PoseBusters Benchmark set, a test set that is potentially harder for methods that might have overfit to their training data because it contains only complexes that the DL methods have not been trained on, GOLD and AutoDock Vina are the best methods in terms of RMSD alone and, when taking physical plausibility into account, or when proteins with novel sequences are considered.
The DL-based methods make few valid predictions for the “unseen” complexes and their performance degrades the more dissimilar the task is from their training data.
Overall, I show that none of the DL-based methods I considered yet outperforms standard docking methods when physical plausibility is taken into account.
Five DL-based and two classical docking methods were used to re-dock known ligands into their respective proteins, and the predicted ligand poses were evaluated with the PoseBusters test suite.
The following section describes the docking methods, the data sets, and the PoseBusters test suite for checking physicochemical consistency and structural plausibility of the generated poses.

The selected five DL-based docking methods (Corso et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2022; Méndez-Lucio et al., 2021; Stärk et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023) cover a wide range of DL-based approaches for pose pre- diction.

In order to examine the ability of standard non-DL-based methods to predict accurate chemically and physically valid poses, I also included the well-established docking methods AutoDock Vina (Forli et al., 2016) and GOLD (Verdonk et al., 2003).

Full details of each can be found in their respective references.
DeepDock (Méndez-Lucio et al., 2021) learns a statistical potential based on the distance likelihood between ligand heavy atoms and points of the mesh of the surface of the binding pocket.
DiffDock (Corso et al., 2023) uses equivariant graph neural networks in a diffusion process for blind docking.
EquiBind (Stärk et al., 2022) applies equivariant graph neural networks for blind docking.
TankBind (Lu et al., 2022) is a blind docking method that uses a trigonometry-aware neural network for docking in each pocket predicted by a binding pocket prediction method.
Uni-Mol (Zhou et al., 2023) carries out docking with SE(3)-equivariant transformers.
All five DL-based docking methods are trained on subsets of the PDBbind 2020 General Set (Z. Liu et al., 2017) as detailed in Table 2.2.
DeepDock is trained on v2019 and the other four are trained on v2020.
It should be noted that I used the DL models as trained by the respective authors without further hyper-parameter tuning.
The docking protocols that were used to generate predictions with each method and the software versions used are given in Appendix B, Section B.2.
Table 2.3 lists the search space definitions that I used for each method.
DeepDock and Uni-Mol require the definition of a binding site while DiffDock, EquiBind, and TankBind are ‘blind’ docking methods that search the entire protein.

I used the default search spaces for the DL-based methods but larger than default search spaces for AutoDock Vina and GOLD, and Uni-Mol such to make them more comparable with the blind docking methods.
Figure 2.1 shows the search spaces for one example protein-ligand complex.
I show results for Uni-Mol across a range of binding site definitions starting from their preferred definition of all residues with an atom within 6 Å of a heavy atom of the crystal ligand.
Under this tight pocket definition Uni-Mol performs better than any of the blind docking methods (Appendix B, Figure B.18).
The PoseBusters test suite is organised into three groups of tests.
The first checks chemical validity and contains tests for the chemical validity and consistency relative to the input.
The second group checks intramolecular properties and tests for the ligand geometry and the ligand conformation’s energy computed using the Universal Force Field (UFF) (Rappe et al., 1992).
The third group considers intermolecular interactions and checks for protein-ligand and ligand-cofactor clashes.
Descriptions of all the tests PoseBusters performs in the three sections are listed in Table 2.4.
Molecule poses which pass all tests in PoseBusters are ‘PB-valid’.

For evaluating docking predictions, PoseBusters requires three input files: an SDF file containing the re-docked ligands, an SDF file containing the true “reference” ligand(s), and a PDB file containing the protein with any cofactors.
The three files are loaded into RDKit molecule objects with the sanitisation option turned off.
The first test in PoseBusters checks whether the ligand passes the RDKit’s sanitisation.

The RDKit’s sanitisation processes information on the valency, aromaticity, radicals, conjugation, hydridization, chirality tags, and protonation to check whether a molecule can be represented as an octet-complete true molecule.

Passing the RDKit’s sanitisation is a commonly-used test for chemical validity in cheminformatics, for example in de novo molecular generation (Brown et al., 2019).

The next test in PoseBusters checks for docking-relevant chemical consistency between the pre- dicted and the true ligands by generating ‘standard InChI’ strings (Heller et al., 2015) for the input and output ligands after removing isotopic information and neutralising charges by adding or removing hydrogens where possible.

InChI is the de facto standard for molecular comparison (Goodman et al., 2021), and the ‘standard InChI’ strings generated include the layers for the molecular formula (/), molecular bonds (/c), hydrogens (/h), net charge (/q), protons (/p), tetrahedral chirality (/t), and double bond stereochemistry (/b).
Standardisation of the ligand’s protonation and charge state is needed because the stereochemistry layer is dependent on the hydrogen (/h), net charge (/q) and proton (/p) layers.
These can unexpectedly change during docking even though most docking software considers the charge distribution and protonation state of a ligand as fixed (Torres et al., 2019).
The normalisation protocol also removes the stereochemistry information of double bonds in primary ketimines which only depends on the hydrogen atom’s ambiguous location.

The first set of physical plausibility tests in the PoseBusters test suite validates bond lengths, bond angles, and internal distances between non-covalently bound pairs of atoms in the docked ligand against the corresponding limits in the distance bounds matrix obtained from the RDKit’s Distance Geometry module.
To pass the tests, all molecular measurements must lie within the user-specified tolerances.

The tolerance used throughout this manuscript is 25 % for bond lengths and bond angles and 30 % for non-covalently bound pairs of atoms e.g.: if a bond is less than 75 % of the Distance Geometry bond length lower bound, it is treated as anomalous.
This was selected as all but one of the crystal ligands in the Astex Diverse set and all of those in the PoseBusters Benchmark set pass at this threshold.

The PoseBusters test for flatness checks that groups of atoms lie in a plane by calculating the closest plane to the atoms and checking that all atoms are within a user-defined distance from this plane.
This test is performed for 5- and 6-membered aromatic rings and non-ring non-aromatic carbon-carbon double bonds.
The chosen threshold of 0.25 Å admits all Astex Diverse and PoseBusters Benchmark set crystal structures by a wide margin, and as with all other thresholds, can be adjusted by the user.
The final test for intramolecular physicochemical plausibility carried out by PoseBusters is an energy calculation to detect highly strained or unlikely conformations.
Our metric for this is the ratio of the energy of the docked ligand conformation to the mean of the energies of a set of 50 generated unconstrained conformations as in Wills et al. (2023).

The conformations are generated using the RDKit’s ETKDGv3 conformation generator (Riniker & Landrum, 2015) followed by a force field relaxation using the UFF (Rappe et al., 1992) and up to 200 iterations.
The test suite rejects conformations for which this ratio is larger than a user-specified threshold.
Wills et al. (2023) set a ratio of seven based on the value where 95 % of the crystal ligands in the PDBbind 2020 General set are considered plausible (Wills et al., 2023).
I selected a less strict ratio of 100 where only one structure each from the Astex Diverse and PoseBusters Benchmark set is rejected.
Intermolecular interactions are evaluated by two sets of tests in the PoseBusters test suite.
The first set checks the minimum distance between molecules and the second checks the share of overlapping volume.
Both sets of tests report on intermolecular interactions of the ligand with four types of molecules: the protein, organic cofactors, and inorganic cofactors.
For the distance-based intermolecular tests PoseBusters calculates the ratio of the pairwise distance between pairs of heavy atoms of two molecules and the sum of the two atoms’ van der Waals radii.
If this ratio is smaller than a user-defined threshold then the test fails.
The default threshold is 0.75 for all pairings.
For inorganic cofactor-ligand pairings the covalent radii are used.
All crystal structures in the Astex Diverse set and all but one in the PoseBusters Benchmark set pass at this threshold.
The van der Waals and covalent radii used are from the Blue Obelisk open data project (O’Boyle, Guha et al., 2011) that the RDKit uses.

For the second set of intermolecular checks, PoseBusters calculates the share of the van der Waals volume of the heavy atoms of the ligand that overlaps with the van der Waals volume of the heavy atoms of the protein using the RDKit’s ShapeTverskyIndex function.
The tests have a configurable scaling factor for the volume-defining van der Waals radii and a threshold that defines how much overlap constitutes a clash.
A threshold is necessary because many crystal structures already contain clashes.
For example, Verdonk et al. (2003) found that 81 out of 305 selected high-quality protein-ligand complexes from the PDB contained steric clashes (Verdonk et al., 2003).
The overlap threshold is 7.5 % for all molecule pairings and the scaling factor is 0.8 for protein-ligand and organic cofactor-ligand pairings and 0.5 for inorganic cofactor-ligand pairings.

PoseBusters calculates the minimum heavy-atom symmetry-aware root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between the predicted ligand binding mode and the closest crystallographic ligand using the RDKit’s GetBestRMS function.
Coverage, a metric often used for testing docking methods, is the share of predictions that are within a user adjustable threshold which by default is 2 Å RMSD.
This value is arbitrary but commonly-used and recommended for regular-size ligands (Cole et al., 2005).
In this chapter, sequence identity between two amino acid chains is the number of exact residue matches after sequence alignment divided by the number of residues of the query sequence.

The sequence alignment used is the Smith–Waterman algorithm (T. Smith & Waterman, 1981) implemented in Biopython (Cock et al., 2009) using an open gap score of −11 and an extension gap score of −1 and the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix.
Unknown amino acid residues are counted as mismatches.

Post-docking energy minimisation of the ligand structure in the binding pocket was performed using the AMBER ff14sb force field (Maier et al., 2015) and the Sage small molecule force field (Boothroyd et al., 2023) in OpenMM (Eastman et al., 2017).
The protein files were prepared using PDBfixer (Eastman et al., 2017) and all protein atom positions were fixed in space only allowing updates to the ligand atoms’ positions.
Minimisation was performed until energy convergence within 0.01 kJ mol−1 per iteration.
The Astex Diverse set (Hartshorn et al., 2007) published in 2007 is a set of hand-picked, relevant, diverse, and high-quality protein-ligand complexes from the PDB (Berman et al., 2000).

The complexes were downloaded from the PDB as MMTF files (Bradley et al., 2017) and PyMOL (DeLano, 2002) was used to remove solvents and all occurrences of the ligand of interest from the complexes before saving the proteins with the cofactors in PDB files and the ligands in SDF files.
I created the PoseBusters Benchmark set, a new set of carefully-selected publicly-available crystal complexes from the PDB.
It is a diverse set of recent high-quality protein-ligand complexes which contain drug-like molecules.
It only contains complexes released since 2021 and therefore does not contain any complexes present in the PDBbind 2020 General set used to train many of the methods.

In this chapter, I discuss PoseBusters, a test suite designed and built to identify chemically inconsistent and physically implausible ligand poses predicted by protein-ligand docking and molecular generation methods.

I show the results of applying the PoseBusters test suite to the output of seven different docking methods, five current DL-based docking methods (DeepDock, DiffDock, EquiBind, TankBind, and Uni-Mol) and two classical docking methods (AutoDock Vina and GOLD).
As mentioned earlier, none of the DL-based docking methods assessed here yet outperforms classical docking methods when both physical plausibility and binding mode RMSD is taken into account.

Our work demonstrates the need for physical plausibility to be taken into account when assessing docking tools because it is possible to perform well on an RMSD-based metric while predicting physically implausible ligand poses (Figure 2.2).

Using the tests in the PoseBusters test suite as an additional criterion when developing DL-based docking methods will help improve methods and the development of more accurate and realistic predictions.
In addition, the individual tests in the PoseBusters test suite highlight docking-relevant failure modes.
The results show that Uni-Mol, for example, predicts non-standard bond lengths and TankBind creates internal ligand clashes.

As mentioned earlier, the ability to identify such failure modes in predicted ligand poses makes PoseBusters a helpful tool for developers to identify inductive biases that could improve their binding mode prediction methods.
Our results also show that, unlike classical docking methods, DL-based docking methods do not generalise well to novel data.

The performance of the DL-based methods on the PoseBusters Benchmark set overall was poor and the subset of the PoseBusters Benchmark set with low sequence identity to PDBbind 2020 General set revealed that DL-based methods are prone to overfitting to the proteins they were trained on.

Our analysis of the targets with sequence identity lower than 30 % to any member of PDBbind 2020 General set revealed that across all of the DL-based docking methods almost no physically valid poses were generated within the 2 Å threshold.

The most commonly-used train-test approach for building DL-based docking models is time-based, e.g., complexes released before a certain date are used for training and complexes released later for testing.
Based on our results, I argue that this is insufficient for testing generalisation to novel targets and the sequence identity between the proteins in the training and test must be reported on.
Post-docking energy minimisation of the ligand using force fields can considerably improve the docking poses generated by DL-based methods.
However, even with an energy minimisation step, the best DL-based method, DiffDock, does not outperform classical docking methods like GOLD and AutoDock Vina.
This shows that at least some key aspects of chemistry and physics encoded in classical docking methods and force fields are missing from DL models.

The PoseBusters test suite provides a new criterion, PB-validity, beyond the traditional “RMSD ⩽ 2 Å” criterion to evaluate the predictions of new DL-based methods, and hopefully will help to identify inductive biases needed for the field to improve docking and molecular generation methods, ultimately resulting in more accurate and realistic predictions.

The next generation of DL-based docking methods should aim to outperform standard docking tools on both RMSD criteria and in terms of chemical consistency, physical plausibility, and generalisability.
This chapter introduced the PoseBusters test suite which can check the generated output of docking methods for chemical consistency and physical plausibility.

The main results from our analysis of five DL-based docking methods are that no DL-based method yet outperforms standard docking methods when considerations of physical plausibility are taken into account, that the DL-based docking methods tested do not generalize to novel data, and that force fields contain docking specific information that is lacking from these DL-based docking methods.
The PoseBusters test suite is a new standard to test for physical plausibility alongside native binding mode accuracy.

Since the publication of the results in this chapter (Buttenschoen et al., 2024), many new DL based docking models, but more broadly also other molecular modelling software, like co-folding methods (Abramson et al., 2024; Boitreaud et al., 2024; Krishna et al., 2024; Wohlwend et al., 2024) and de novo molecular generation methods (Buttenschoen et al., 2025; M. Li et al., 2025) have been assessed using the PoseBusters test suite.

The tests have become a tool for method developers to check that their methods do not egregiously violate stereochemistry and physics, and have helped identify the inductive biases still required to improve DL-based docking methods, as shown by recent improvements (Corso et al., 2024).
Since the publication of the first version of the PoseBusters software, additional tests have been added and bugs have been fixed based on suggestions and feedback from various users.

For example, Errington et al. (2025) have expanded the set of metrics by monitoring the conservation of intermolecular interactions, showing another way to possibly improve DL-based protein-ligand models, namely by training models directly to learn intermolecular interactions.

In this chapter, I describe how I used the PoseBusters tests developed in the previous chapter to also assess the models’ training and test data.
The models’ failure modes are present in the commonly used training data set PDBbind 2020 General set, but not as strongly pronounced.
The high quality of the established test sets, the Astex Diverse set, CASF-2016, and PoseBusters Benchmark set, is reconfirmed.

A well-known adage in computer science is “garbage in, garbage out.” In the context of machine learning, this principle implies that low-quality training data will tend to produce low-quality models.
This concern is even more pronounced for deep learning, which seeks to learn meaningful latent representations directly from data.
Consequently, a comprehensive evaluation of deep learning-based docking models must also consider the quality of the experimental structures used in training.

Experimentally-solved structures of protein-ligand complexes can vary significantly in quality, and this includes the resolution of the experimental structures (see Appendix A, Section A.1.4), the quality of model fit, and the completeness of the ligand models.

The Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al., 2000), introduced in Chapter 1 as the most important source of experimentally-derived protein-ligand structures, has been continuously growing and now, at the end of 2025, it contains approximately 170 000 protein-ligand structures.
However, not all of these structures are suitable for method development, which is why subsets of relevant, representative, and high quality structures from the PDB are typically selected.
Some data sets that have been used for the training and evaluation of docking methods are listed in Section 3.1.

Not only the quality, but also the volume of the training data is important.
The first method to use linear regression to predict binding affinity in docking was AutoDock 3, which used 30 protein-ligand complexes (Morris et al., 1998), for a model with 5 parameters.
DL-based methods, with billions of parameters to be fitted, require far more training data, but it is not yet clear how much data is needed.
The largest data set I have seen used to train DL-base docking models in Section 3.1 is BindingMOAD, which contains 41 409 protein-ligand complexes.
Not only data selection, but also data preparation is important for many docking workflows.

Ligand preparation includes creating 3D coordinates, adding hydrogen atoms, setting charges, assigning proper bond orders, and generating accessible tautomers, while receptors are typically prepared by removing atom clashes, filling in missing atoms and residues, placing waters, and optimising hydrogen bonds (Sastry et al., 2013).

For classical docking, data preparation has been shown to critically influence docking success rates, with small preparation errors causing fluctuations of more than 20 % in docking success rates (Corbeil et al., 2012).
The representation and parsing of molecular data is not a trivial problem, in part because several cheminformatics file formats in common use are not open standards.
For example, the widely used MOL2 file format is defined by a closed-source implementation in proprietary software, and no complete public specification exists.
As a result, developers of independent software have had to infer or reconstruct parts of the format, which has led to incompatibilities.
For this reason, the most commonly used open-source cheminformatics library, the RDKit, does not support saving molecules in the MOL2 format.
Another example is the PDB file format, which allows molecules to be stored without explicit bond order information or atomic charges.
This missing information can cause difficulties when parsing molecular structures upon loading.
When DL–based models are trained on such poorly specified data, it is therefore prudent to verify the molecular structures that are actually loaded from the data set.
If problems are identified, the choice of training data and the associated quality criteria should be re-examined.
Benchmarking the RDKit is important because it is the de facto standard cheminformatics library.
It is used by all five DL–based docking methods evaluated in the previous chapter.
The RDKit’s strengths include its robustness, active maintenance, rich feature set, high-performance C++ backend, user-friendly Python API, and extensive documentation.
However, users must exercise caution.

The RDKit performs strict parsing of molecular files and does not attempt to infer missing information, such as atomic charges, bond orders, or valence states, that are not explicitly specified in the input.

While this behaviour increases reliability and transparency, it also means that data sets that cannot be loaded correctly by the RDKit warrant careful scrutiny, particularly given the widespread adoption of the library.

First, I consider what the results show in regards to the ‘garbage in, garbage out’ hypothesis.
As the results show, the PDBbind 2020 General training data set does have a large number of structures that do not pass the tests.
The most severe structural failure mode is protein-ligand clash (Appendix C, Figure C.6a).
This is shared with the five previously benchmarked DL-based models that were trained on subsets of the PDBbind 2020 General General set (Chapter 2, Table 2.2).
However, when comparing failure rates of the methods (Figures C.7 and C.8) to those in the data sets, I observe higher failure rates (Appendix C, Tables 3.2 and 3.3).

In particular, the methods generate poses with much higher protein- ligand clash rates from the DL-based methods compared to the training data (Figure 3.3) and while the training data does contain systematic structural artefacts, these data issues alone cannot explain the observed error rates in the predicted poses.

In conclusion, there is some evidence that these DL-based models learn protein-ligand clashes from the data, but the quality of the training data does not fully explain the much higher failure rates observed in the models.
To discern the influence of problematic data on model performance, it is not sufficient to examine the training data alone.
One could retrain the models on filtered clean versions of the training data set to see what the effect of the faulty data really is.
However, it is likely that incorrect handling and loading of the data might have caused some of the models to learn from faulty molecular representations.
Indeed, the results show that loading molecular data sets with the RDKit is not trivial.
Depending on which files are chosen and on what options are used, one might get 91 % passing protein-ligand complexes or none when loading the molecules of the CASF-2016 data set.
In general, there is no molecular file type from which the RDKit is guaranteed to load valid molecules.

All file formats admit underspecified or wrong molecular data, and the RDKit parser, as noted, although known for particularly strict parsing, cannot follow the unwritten conventions of other software when dealing with omitted information.
When the RDKit cannot sanitise a molecule, an error is raised.
However, when no error is raised, a molecule can still be wrong.
This is because sanitization does not guarantee that the molecule was correctly loaded.
These silent bugs are logic errors, and they cause molecules to be parametrised wrongly.
This happens when loading the CASF-2016 files.

When loading the SDF files of the ligands instead of the MOL2 files, there are some sanitisation errors, but other ligands load without error but have radicals, non-flat double bonds, and flat non-aromatic rings and their internal energies are much too large (Appendix C, Figure C.4).
This happens despite the two molecular file formats containing identical coordinates and atom types.
The reason is that two different molecules end up being loaded by the RDKit: one is correct, and the other is incorrect.
The wrong chemical representation causes a faulty parametrisation of the UFF in the energy ratio test, leading to a downstream error caused by the file being misinterpreted by the RDKit.

Clearly, the chemical representation of the molecules matters a lot, and much care must be taken to load molecules correctly with the RDKit, because learning from chemically faulty data possibly limits the methods’ performance.

In summary, special care must be taken when loading molecular files with the RDKit - some substructures, such as four valent nitrogens, are never correctly loaded and could lead to systematic blind spots.
Obtaining the latest data from the PDB in mmCIF format and regenerating the data set, as was done for the Astex Diverse, was successful.
The molecular structures loaded from the original files with RDKit were only 60 % PB-valid, but the recreated Astex Diverse set was 92 % PB-valid.

It is apparent that high quality filters (e.g. maximum resolution of 2.5 Å), for example those used to select structures for the Astex Diverse set, the CASF-2016 set, and the PoseBusters Benchmark set, did indeed yield higher quality data selections, even though the PoseBusters tests were not used directly as criteria.
As the PDB continually expands and the RDKit is continually improved, regenerating the data sets periodically will be important.
For future work, it would be interesting to study the diversity and uniqueness of the data.
The PDBbind 2020 General contains 19 443 protein-ligand complexes from the PDB, of which 155 are redundant leaving 19 288 complexes.
For training generative models, it is important not only to have diverse data that do not repeat, but also to have data that cover as much of the input space as possible.
Describing the distribution of the data in terms of diversity measured by protein sequence identity or ligand similarity will be important.
Further work for understanding the trade-off between using all data and selecting only high quality data would be a useful step.

This is because showing that the training data have the same failure modes as the models is only a necessary but not sufficient condition to show that the models have learnt the problems from the data.
Retraining the models with cleaner data would allow this to be measured.
It would be interesting to see what effect retraining the DL-based docking methods on cleaner data sets would have.
This would give a signal of whether efforts to improve the structure models of the PDB, via refitting the models on the electron densities, could be worthwhile for model developers.
In conclusion, the results showed that data sets of molecular structures obtained from the PDB should be carefully inspected, filtered, and errors corrected.
Although the failure modes of the DL-based docking methods resembled those of the training data, I find that the training data were of better quality than the model predictions would make us believe.
To fully discern the influence of problematic data on model performance, the models could be retrained on filtered versions of the data set and their results be compared.
Further, I recommend that all practitioners benchmark and carefully select the training data they choose to build DL-based docking models, maybe less is more in some cases.
In this chapter, I explore common patterns in structure-based drug design using a large collection of protein-ligand complex pairs from the PDB.

The chapter describes the process of selecting high-quality complexes from the PDB, aligning the pairs of PDB structures around ligands bound in the same binding site of the same protein receptors, the measurements calculated on the structures, and the patterns observed in the data.
The chapter provides extensive experimental evidence for an important concept in medicinal chemistry, which is that molecules with similar structures have similar binding modes.
This provides a starting point for the guidance of docking models introduced in the following chapter.
Structure-based drug discovery often relies on the tacit knowledge acquired by practitioners over multiple projects with specific protein-ligand systems.

This knowledge includes the binding modes of existing lead series, the flexibility of the protein and its binding pocket, and the effect of structural changes in the ligand on binding mode and affinity.
Central to this is the dogma that similar molecules with similar structures have similar properties (Deane, 1990).

Molecular modellers and medicinal chemists with relevant experience can recognise familiar patterns in interactions and substructures, which they use to generate new ideas to improve the binding and properties of lead compounds (Bissantz et al., 2010).
The medicinal chemistry literature makes some of this knowledge explicit.

Individual case studies of success stories in structure-based drug discovery include those of approved drugs such as vemurafenib (AlKharboush et al., 2025) and current candidates in clinical studies such as AMG 510 (Lanman et al., 2020) and are important reading for practitioners working on the same targets.
Data science approaches have also been applied to make medicinal chemistry knowledge explicit in the context of structure-based drug discovery.

For example, Ferreira de Freitas and Schapira (2017) studied the frequency distribution of non-covalent interactions in a set of 11 016 PDB structures and highlighted how the addition of one interaction may cause structurally similar ligands with conserved binding poses to differ significantly in binding affinity.

Malhotra and Karanicolas (2017) found that only in 14 % of 297 pairs of assembled smaller and larger ligands the binding mode definitely changes upon chemical elaboration, and in many of these the change is due to an expansion of the smaller molecule of the pair into the space occupied by the receptor.

Giangreco et al. (2013) collected 121 molecular overlays from the PDB that support the pharmacophoric hypothesis, namely that structurally diverse molecules with chemical features arranged similarly in space can bind to the same target.

In the context of fragment-based drug design, Drwal et al. (2018) found that in a set of 3672 structures containing fragments and their drug-like superstructures, smaller chemical changes lead to retention of the binding mode more frequently than larger ones.
Although such insights are valuable and can guide practitioners, this is familiar knowledge to expert medicinal chemists.
What such experts need are the right tools to put their structural hypotheses to the test when optimising compounds.
To this end, classical pose prediction tools allow users to bias the predictions (Paggi et al., 2024).
For example, the Python API of the docking program GOLD (Verdonk et al., 2003) allows the specification of distance constraints for individual atoms.
However, many recently developed DL-based docking tools still lack such a capability.

In order to address this limitation, and in preparation for training and testing DL-based methods on the structure-based hypotheses that medicinal chemists employ, I set out to collect a large number of pairs of ligands bound to the same binding site from the PDB.

Although I could start with a data set curated for studying protein-ligand interaction patterns and binding modes, such as the sc-PDB (Kellenberger et al., 2006) which contains 16 034 carefully protonated and chemically-complete complexes in its latest iteration (Desaphy et al., 2015), I start with the PDB as it is the largest and fastest growing data set of experimentally resolved protein-ligand structures.

By the end of 2017, which is the year of the latest release of the sc-PDB, the PDB contained 111 874 structures obtained by X-ray crystallography and this number has nearly doubled and currently contains 246 715 structures, as noted in Chapter 1, including more than 450 000 protein-ligand interactions (Durairaj et al., 2024).

In this chapter, I explore the data set with a hypothesis-driven data science approach to test whether the data make sense and to quantify the degree to which molecules with similar structures have similar binding modes.
In the next chapter, I will test and develop machine learning-based drug development tools using these data.

Because protein chains in PDB structures do not use a standardised residue numbering scheme, residues were mapped between structures using the sequence alignments generated previously for the structural alignments.

The pairs of ligands were categorised according to the following definitions: A pair of ligands is identical if the ligand has the same CCD identifier in the PDB file or if the standard InChI strings (Heller et al., 2015) generated for the molecules are identical.
A pair of ligands is an elaboration if the MCS is one of the ligands.
Following Malhotra and Karanicolas (2017), a pair of ligand poses is conserved when SCRDKit is at least 80 %.

Overall, 232 665 unique pairs of PDB structures with ligands bound to the same protein and the same binding pocket were collected, and 53 048 (23 %) of these are pairs of identical ligands bound to the same receptor (but still in different PDB structures).
Of the 179 617 pairs containing non-identical ligands, 99 319 (55 %) pairs contain fragments, 3698 (2.1 %) pairs are elaborations, and 2587 (1.4 %) contain fragment elaborations.
Further, 92 255 (51 %) of the non-identical pairs contain drug-like molecules and 46 159 (26 %) pairs contain a pair of a fragment and a drug-like ligand.
Binding poses are more commonly conserved in pairs of chemically similar ligands.

Figure 4.1 shows the shape and pharmacophoric similarity, measured by SCRDKit , of all pairs of non-identical pairs of ligands (179 617) versus chemical similarity, measured via chemical fingerprints.
The plot shows that, for more chemically similar pairs of ligands, the binding pose is conserved more commonly.
It also shows a high similarity of H-bond interactions (yellow) for chemically dissimilar ligands.
Figure 4.2 shows the same set of non-identical pairs (179 617) binned by chemical similarity and in terms of the percentage of poses conserved (SCRDKit ≥ 0.8).
This plot shows the trend more clearly; clearly, there is a steady increase in the percentage of poses conserved as a function of chemical similarity.
For ligand pairs with chemical similarity larger than 80 %, around 90 % of the observed pairs in the data set have conserved binding modes.
Of the 53 048 pairs of identical ligands, 99.0 % are pairs that conserve the binding mode (SCRDKit ≥ 0.8) and 1.0 % (527) do not conserve binding mode (SCRDKit < 0.8).
Six of those pairs of structures containing identical ligands (identical CCD identifiers) with non-conserved poses are shown in Figures D.3 and D.4.
Three of these poses are distinctly different (Figures D.3a and D.4c and Section D.4).

The publications of the PDB structures reveal that ligand DGT in structures 4TNX and 4TO6 is an allosteric binder, ligand DIF binds is shown in different species (6HN0 is ovine and 6HN1 is caprine serum albumin), and ligand OCF receptors 8AYJ and 8ONN differ by a point mutation.
This might explain some pairs of poses scoring lower than expected (Figure D.3b).
Similarly, three of the pairs of ligands with identical CCD identifiers have have non-identical Fingerprints (2048-bit ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity less than 1, for example Figure D.4c).

The ECFPs (2048-bit, radius 2) used here also distinguish ligands with different protonation patterns, resulting in some ligand pairs with identical CCD identifiers scoring less than one in terms of fingerprint similarity.
