My analysis shows that chemical similarity correlates strongly with pose conservation, as shown in Figures 4.1 and 4.2.
This agrees with the approach often used in structure-based drug design.
Small changes in molecular structures often maintain the binding modes of the original structures more often than larger ones.
In particular, elaborations of molecules maintain binding modes very often; more than 80 % of all observed elaborations maintain the binding pose.
This agrees with the main principle of structural medicinal chemistry, that is making small changes to lead compounds and existing scaffolds.

The statistic that 99.0 % identical ligands conserve their binding pose in the same pocket of different PDB structures confirms how consistent the binding events observed in the crystal structures are.
However, the remaining pairs (1.0 %, 527) include pairs with significant changes in the binding mode when bound to the same receptor (Section D.4).

Slightly different protonation patterns affected the ECFP4 fingerprints, but spot checks revealed that point mutations, difference in pH of the crystal, re- ceptors from different species, and allosteric binding might cause these differences.
The 90 % sequence identity threshold for pairing protein receptors does not filter pose-relevant point mutations.
Identical fragments have been observed elsewhere to adopt multiple binding poses (Malhotra & Karanicolas, 2017).
Initially, perhaps surprisingly, in our data, pairs of identical fragments have a high rate (99.7 %) of pose conservation.
However, this does not mean that fragments do not adopt multiple poses, because in our pair selection process, I only choose the combination of ligand poses that leads to the highest SCRDKit .
When there were multiple fragments in a binding site, I chose the pair with the pose that was the most similar.
This explains the high rate of pose conservation in identical fragments.
Fragment elaboration pairs showed a similar high rate of pose conservation as all elaboration pairs.
The trends observed for the MCS also agree with intuition: If more of a ligand is conserved, and if fewer atoms are added, then the more similar the smaller and larger ligand poses are.
However, the fitted model on smaller ligand size, relative MCS size, and number of atoms added only explained about 33 % of the variance observed in pose similarity (Pseudo 𝑅2 = 0.33).
The missing variation might be explained by the amount of chemical complementarity removed and added, which was not represented in these models.
Intermolecular interactions are directly related to binding affinity.

For this reason, medicinal chemists count interactions and add up their contributions when designing structures, as can be gleaned from average interaction strength tables (Burnell et al., 2016, Table 3.1, p. 32).
The correlations between interactions and pose conservation were lower than expected.
Almost no positive correlation is observed (Figure 4.13); the hydrogen bond interaction type has the highest Spearman correlation, which is almost negligible at 𝜌 = 0.08.
This suggests that pharmacophores and interactions contain orthogonal information and should both be considered when designing.

The data set used in this study has a positive selection bias, as I have selected pairs of protein-ligand complexes for which experimentally resolved structures of both ligands bound within the same pocket of the same protein exist.
A modification of a molecule that failed to lead to a binding event in the same binding site (or did not bind at all) would not be represented in our data.
Another bias in our study is that the chemical space represented here is the one explored by structural experiments that led to the submission of structures to the PDB.
These experiments do not explore the proteomic and chemical space uniformly, and only a very small subspace of combinations of ligands and proteins can ever be explored.
A further limitation of this analysis is that most PDB structures do not contain biologically accurate protonation patterns of receptors and ligands.
Similarly, the hydrogen bonds in water networks of binding sites are mostly unresolved in experimental structures.
Although I know that the solvation and protonation patterns strongly contribute to protein-ligand binding, I did not have the data to analyse these here.
In this chapter, I conducted a study of the protein-ligand binding patterns of pairs of structures of similar ligands bound to the same pocket in the same protein from the PDB.
My analysis shows that ligands with high chemical similarity conserve binding modes more frequently and that elaborations, on average, conserve poses more frequently.
Interaction metrics are found to correlate with chemical similarity, but not with pharmacophoric measurements.
This chapter provided some insight into the types of biases that medicinal chemists use when performing structure-based drug design.
It also provides a large data set for the study of protein-ligand patterns that can be further explored.
In the next chapter, I use a diverse subset of these paired data to steer a DL-based docking model to conserve user-chosen interactions and substructures.
Until now, I have explored protein-ligand interactions through docking models (Chapter 2) and paired crystallographic data (Chapter 4).
Now we turn to applying our insights and improving deep learning (DL)-based docking.

In this chapter, I start with the DL-based model that performed best in the benchmark in Chapter 2, namely DiffDock (Corso et al., 2023), and apply diffusion guidance to inject user constraints and physical information into the diffusion process.

I first demonstrate on a series of test setups that this approach only produces predictions in the binding site when given the binding pocket location (a user constraint), that the force field information (physical information) improves physical plausibility, and that substructure and interaction constraints (user constraints) can be met with high precision.
In our experiments, I also find that gradient-based guidance performs slightly better than gradient-free guidance.
Next, a realistic docking benchmark is set up in which ligands cross-dock into cognate receptor structures of chemically similar ligands, as is custom in lead optimisation.

I demonstrate the performance of our approach on this task using a new data set of public PDB structures and on a set of unpublished cereblon binding molecular glues with unpublished interactions and an unpublished target.
The resulting method is named GuideDock.

When medicinal chemists use docking for virtual screening, they formulate design hypotheses and select ligands accordingly; for example, they might select ligands that share a certain substructure with a lead molecule for which an experimental protein-ligand complex is available.

For some hypotheses, the medicinal chemists might be able to define constraints; in the previous example, this would be to constrain the atoms of the shared substructures in the same positions during cross-docking.
Such constraints allow a user to test their design hypotheses, but they might also lead to better predicted poses.

Although classical docking methods such as AutoDock 4 (Morris et al., 2009) and GOLD (Ver- donk et al., 2003) support atom-wise position constraints suitable for this example, dedicated methods such as EnzyDock (Das et al., 2019), EDock (W. Zhang et al., 2020), and FitDock (X. Yang et al., 2022) can extract these constraints from template ligands.
DL-based docking models do not yet support any constraints, despite their potential practicality, and even though well-informed constraints can improve docking results.
To test how well DL-based methods might perform with constraints, I integrate constraints into the best DL-based model according to our comparison in Chapter 2.
The chosen base model is DiffDock, an SE(3) Riemannian diffusion model.
For diffusion models, in general, there are multiple approaches to add constraints.

Due to computational constraints, I restricted myself to training-free approaches, which only modify the inference procedure and avoid the computationally costly training of models by re-using model weights fitted by others.
Of course, this excludes approaches that modify the functional form of the model (Didi et al., 2023) or propose alternative loss functions (Didi et al., 2023).

At the time of starting this work, training-free approaches had not yet been implemented for biological structural models, but I became aware of them in the domain of image generation (Bansal et al., 2023; Lugmayr et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2024) and I sought to adopt that approach for DiffDock.
However, in the meantime, approaches similar to ours have been implemented in co-folding methods (Boitreaud et al., 2024; Wohlwend et al., 2024).
Defining constraints when modelling biological structures is a well known procedure in the adjacent field of molecular dynamics.

Here, distance constraints are often used to prevent or enforce interactions, while position constraints can be used to anchor a structure in place to prevent it from drifting out of the frame (Eastman et al., 2024).

In molecular dynamics simulations, soft constraints are typically implemented as additional terms in the force field, for example, as an additional harmonic term with its minimum at a desired atom location.
Force fields are differentiable scalar functions of the positions of the atoms, and they are parametrised using the molecular structures in the system of interest.
The energy functions in classical force fields are linear functions that sum up terms of various energetic contributions such as bond stretching and steric clashes.
Rather than just adopting the constraint terms, I build a system that can flexibly include any differentiable scalar function on atom positions, which includes all force fields by definition.
Our motivation is two-fold.

First, I hope that guidance with the non-constraint terms will help reduce the number of physically implausible predictions, a problem I identified in Chapter 2, and second, I hope that this setup will make our model easier to use, as users will be familiar with defining constraints on force fields.

To summarise, I tackle three use cases with inference time guidance, illustrated in Figure 5.1: The first is to enable binding site-specific docking with the blind docking model, the second is to allow users to define position and distance constraints, and the third is to improve the physical validity of the predicted poses.
I choose DiffDock-L (Corso et al., 2024), the follow-up method to DiffDock that I benchmarked, as the base model.

DiffDock-L is a blind DL-based docking method that decomposes the docking task like most classical docking methods: into a pose generation model for sampling poses, and a scoring model to rank the generated poses.
During inference, the pose generation model is applied 20 times to sample and transform random noise into a ligand binding pose.
This is done in batch to generate 20 ligand poses.
The scoring model is then applied to rank these predictions.

The pose generation model is an SE(3)-equivariant Riemannian diffusion model that defines a diffusion process over the roto-translations and torsions of the typical docking state-space, and it is trained by score-matching with an exploding variance schedule (Y. Song et al., 2021).
The score model has a very similar architecture, but is trained as a classifier that predicts whether a generated pose is within 2 Å RMSD of the crystal pose.
Both models use graph neural networks with equivariant tensor products (Geiger & Smidt, 2022).

As input, the pose generation model only takes the alpha carbon locations of the receptor proteins into account, ignoring side chains and cofactors, while the scoring model evaluates the poses using all heavy atoms of the protein, also ignoring any cofactors.

Another important limitation, in addition to ignoring anything but protein chains, is the hardcoded limit of 1022 amino acids for the length of the receptor protein chains due to the period of rotary positional embeddings being 1024 for the ESM2 model (Lin et al., 2023), which is used to generate embeddings for residues.
In our benchmark of docking methods (Chapter 2), DiffDock was the best DL-based model.

It showed high physical plausibility in terms of bond lengths, bond angles, and stereochemistry, but protein-ligand clash rates were higher than those of classical docking methods and the main physical failure mode.
DiffDock-L represents an improvement and has 27 % of poses within 2 Å RMSD and PB- valid, relative to 12 % of the poses of DiffDock.
Figure E.1 shows a waterfall plot of the failure modes of DiffDock-L with the most prominent being protein-ligand clash, as it was for DiffDock (Figure B.4e).
In what follows, I apply guidance to the pose generation model of DiffDock-L to control the sampling and improve the quality of the samples generated.
I make no alterations to the pose scoring model.
For both models, I maintain the default inference settings and use the publicly available weights provided by the authors for DiffDock v1.1.3 on the project’s GitHub page.

These weights were generated by Corso et al. (2024) training on BindingMOAD2020 (Hu et al., 2005) which includes most protein-ligand complexes released to the Protein Data Bank (Berman et al., 2000) before 2020.
Guidance is a framework for conditioning generative diffusion models on additional information at inference time.

Various authors have already described guidance for different types of diffusion models for various domains, such as images (Bansal et al., 2023; Lugmayr et al., 2022), audio processing (Ye et al., 2024), and molecular systems (Didi et al., 2023).
For example, in image generation, guidance can be used to condition on a text prompt (Epstein et al., 2023).
Various guidance frameworks for score-based diffusion models have been proposed recently.
Recall that score-based diffusion models (Y. Song et al., 2021) are trained to approximate the score ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥) of a noisy version of the data.

One robust way to create a conditional generative model is to separately train a classifier model on paired data of the form (𝑥, 𝑦) and derive the score ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑦 ∣ 𝑥) from it; the model’s task effectively being to predict the desired property 𝑦 from noisy versions of the data (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021).
By Bayes’ theorem, the sum the two scores ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥) and ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑦 ∣ 𝑥) is the conditional score for ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥 ∣ 𝑦).

Another approach, known as classifier-free guidance, trains on the unconditional and conditional task simultaneously via masking (Ho & Salimans, 2021); this effectively performs score-matching for ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥 ∣ 𝑦) and ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥).
A disadvantage of these approaches is that they require training and that all particular classes of labels that the model should work with must be specified from the beginning.
Training-free guidance, yet another type of guidance, does not change the model but modifies the iteratively generated intermediate predictions during inference.
Essentially, this form of guidance adds an optimisation task at each intermediate (Bansal et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024).

When the conditional score ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑦 ∣ 𝑥) is tractable or good proxies exists, conditioning can be performed using only the unconditional model (Bansal et al., 2023; Chung et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024).
However, while I adopt this approach for being training-free, it has been mentioned that the training-based forms of guidance lead to better results.

The training-free guidance framework used here is akin to Diffusion Posterior Sampling (Chung et al., 2023), Universal Guidance (Bansal et al., 2023), and Training-Free Guidance (Ye et al., 2024) but adapted to DiffDock’s latent space and noise schedule.

The three cited frameworks have been developed for variance preserving score-models (J. Song et al., 2021) in Euclidean spaces, but here I apply the same concept to the sampling model of DiffDock-L, a score model with a variance exploding schedule (Ho et al., 2020) operating on a non-Euclidean state space.

Our goal is not to mathematically derive the general validity of the resulting approach, but to practically show that this approach is possible and to evaluate the merits of guidance for DL-based docking.
A sketch of our approach, using the generic notation of score-based models (Y. Song et al., 2021), follows.
The main idea is that I perform an optimisation of the posterior mean obtained from the latent variables at each inference step.

To clarify, the posterior mean is a point estimate in the target space 𝑥̂0 obtained from the latent 𝑥𝑡 at each inference step using the formula 𝔼 [𝑥0 ∣ 𝑥𝑡 ] = 𝑥𝑡 + 𝜎𝑡2 ∇𝑥𝑡 log 𝑝(𝑥0 ∣ 𝑥𝑡 ), also known as Tweedie’s formula (Efron, 2011).
I obtain the estimator by plugging-in the score model that was trained to approximate the score, which in mathematical notation is S(𝑥𝑡 , 𝑡) ≈ ∇𝑥𝑡 log 𝑝(𝑥0 ∣ 𝑥𝑡 ).
This way I obtain the formula for our estimator 𝑥̂0 which is This estimator is at the centre of the optimisations in the training-free guidance frameworks cited above.
The next step to setup the optimisations is to define a loss function ℓ which can be any differentiable scalar function on the target space of the model.
All force fields for protein-ligand dynamics including constraints fit this description.
The force fields used for our experiments are described in Section 5.2.3.
I investigate two optimisation schemes.
The first is ‘backward’ guidance, in which 𝑥̂0 is optimised without differentiating through the model.
In mathematical notation, the backward guidance optimisation task is The second optimisation scheme is ‘forward’ guidance in which differentiates through the score model.
This requires evaluating the score model and its gradient and is therefore more costly computationally.
However, I investigate this approach because it might lead to better results.

In mathematical notation, the ‘forward’ guidance optimisation task is In practice, optimisation might not be performed at every inference step due to efficiency considerations and numerical stability.

To illustrate the latter, during early time steps, the mean conditional expectation often does not resemble a valid ligand pose, and the ligand might clash with the receptor, leading to very large values of an energy function due to terms that divide by the distance between atoms, e.g. clash terms based on the Lennard-Jones potential.

An important technical detail for implementing this form of guidance for DiffDock-L is that I re- quire an ‘adapter’ function that converts between updates to the internal coordinates and the external coordinates.
This is because when I optimise 𝑥̂0 , I want to optimise using the internal coordinates (to remain on the manifold), but the force field is written in terms of the external coordinates.
DiffDock-L already includes a function 𝒜𝑐 that maps elements of the tangent space of the internal coordinates and a reference ligand conformation to the external coordinates.
Therefore, I only need to implement its inverse, a new function 𝒫𝑐 , which is a function that maps external coordinates and a reference ligand pose to changes in the internal coordinates.

This function may use the same reference conformation 𝑐 that DiffDock-L uses to define its state space, that is, the space spanned by the roto-translations and torsions applied to the reference pose 𝑐.

Clearly, this function must be a projection onto the tangent space of the internal coordinates (the tangent space of the manifold) because the external coordinates are of higher dimensions than the internal ones.

Based on the definition of the translation, rotation, and torsions, we can define 𝒫𝑐 as the inverse of 𝒜𝑐 such that 𝒫𝑐 ⋅ 𝒜𝑐 = I. Let 𝒫𝑐 be defined as applying the same operations of 𝒜𝑐 but in reverse order: first undo the torsions1 in exactly the reverse order, then use the Kabsch algorithm (Kabsch, 1976) to remove the translation and rotation components induced by the torsions, and then recover the rotation and translation with another application of the Kabsch algorithm.
For all optimisations, the LBFGS optimiser (Byrd et al., 1995) of PyTorch (Ansel et al., 2024) was used with a set maximum of 10 iterations and a tolerance of 10−5 as an early stopping criterion.

I investigated the application of training-free guidance to DiffDock for three different goals: constrained docking, binding-site specific docking, and improving the physical validity of the base model.
For constrained and pocket-specific docking, I dock a novel ligand into a related ligand’s cognate re- ceptor, which is similar to how docking is used in lead optimisation for drug discovery.
For constrained docking, I provide a set of atom coordinates obtained from the related ligand in its cognate receptor.
These are within 2 Å of the pose of the aligned new ligands and should provide useful constraints.
For pocket-specific docking, I provide the centroid of the aligned novel ligand as a constraint.

By implementing simple guidance in DiffDock-L, I demonstrated that the predictions of diffusionbased molecular structure models can be steered in a controlled manner.

Using simple loss functions for guidance was sufficient to increase the physical plausibility of generated poses, as evaluated by PoseBusters, while avoiding the expensive parametrisation required for energy minimisation with a full molecular dynamics force field.
I further showed that guidance improves the performance of DiffDock-L not only in terms of phys- ical plausibility but also in accuracy, as measured by RMSD within 2 Å.

Incorporating prior information from related ligands, sometimes referred to as templates, unsurprisingly improved performance for cross-docking, but only when the underlying assumptions of this approach were satisfied.
Crucially, this requires that the imposed constraints do not interfere with docking and that the rigid receptor does not sterically block the correct ligand pose.
Using guidance to enable pocket-specific and constrained docking was shown to work well in practice.
Revealing additional information about the ligand and its binding pose to the model during inference improved performance relative to the base model.
I showed that the same base model can be applied across these different tasks.
However, when compared to the classical docking method GOLD, our models still performed worse in terms of physical plausibility, though not in terms of RMSD accuracy.
Training the base model to generate only PoseBusters-valid poses may therefore be a promising direction.
Overall, the performance of the resulting method, GuideDock, is at best comparable to that of the classical docking method GOLD, both with and without additional constraints.
A more fundamental paradigm shift, such as moving from docking to co-folding, may be required to surpass traditional physical docking methods in a meaningful way.
Our approach uniquely demonstrates how physical terms derived from force fields and userdefined biases can be integrated with state-of-the-art DL methods for rigid small-molecule docking.
The terms used here improve results by incorporating information that the model either did not learn to exploit (physics) or did not have access to (user biases).
Introducing user biases also enables practitioners to directly test their hypotheses within the docking process.
In this chapter I presented GuideDock, a DL-based docking method that innovates by adding diffusion guidance to the DiffDock-L blind docking method.

This allows reusing the pre-trained model to perform constrained docking and pocket-specific docking, while simultaneously also improving the physical plausibility of the generated poses in comparison to the unguided DiffDock.

Although GuideDock does not surpass classical docking methods, in particular the classical docking method GOLD, the experiments demonstrate that repurposing a single blind docking model for multiple different tasks is possible.
Since I started working on GuideDock, other researchers have implemented guidance terms in biological structure prediction models.
The ‘steering’ approach that was added to the second version of the preprint of Boltz (Wohlwend et al., 2024) this summer is very similar to our method.
I am excited that I was on the right track with this work, but I suspect that the machine learning community now views co-folding as having superseded docking.
The aim of this thesis was to investigate deep learning (DL)-based protein–ligand docking.

Motivated by the landmark success of AlphaFold2 in protein structure prediction and by the observation that DL- based docking has not yet achieved a comparable impact, I sought to contribute to the advancement of this field.

In particular, this work aimed to assess the current capabilities of existing methods, identify opportunities for improvement, and support the maturation of DL-based docking as a practical technology.
My research improves our understanding of DL-based protein-ligand docking by investigating the shortcomings of common evaluation metrics, training data, and testing setups.
In addition, my research explored the interplay of physics-based and DL-based approaches and showed that diffusion guidance can inject physical biases and user knowledge.
My first key finding is that the established RMSD metric of being within 2 Å of the crystallographic binding mode is insufficient to assess DL-based protein-ligand docking.
Using examples, I showed that the 2 Å RMSD threshold admits physically impossible pretzel-shaped conformations and stark protein- ligand clashes, among others.
As a remedy, I implemented a new metric, PB-validity, which consists of a series of physical and chemical plausibility tests.
This new metric has been adopted by the research community to benchmark docking, de novo molecular generation, and co-folding models.
My most significant contribution is that I have systematically shown that DL-based docking methods have not yet outperformed classical docking methods.
I did this in two independent ways: first, by creating a new, more difficult test set, the PoseBusters test set; and second, by introducing the new metric: PB-validity.
Both provide unique insights into the performance of the models: The PoseBusters tests enumerate chemical and physical failure modes, telling the user what exactly has gone wrong and how badly.
Independently, using a novel out-of-distribution training data test set and splitting it by sequence identity revealed that DL-based methods generalise less well than classical docking methods.
The impact of this contribution has seen a renewed effort of model developers to improve the physical plausibility of docking as well as co-folding models.

Also important is my finding that the very training data, the crystal structures in the PDBbind 2020 General set (and its successor PDBbind 2020 General R1), are polluted with the same failure modes with which DL-based methods struggle.
Filtering, pre-processing, or remediating the training data is rarely done but should be; this includes double-checking that the molecular representations loaded from the data sets are correct.
A simple way to do this is to use the PoseBusters tests also to inspect the training data, but that alone does not guarantee problem-free structures.

Regarding time-based training-test data splits, I found that time-splits are insufficient to demonstrate generalisation because they omit use case-dependent considerations of target and pocket similarity, ligand similarity and known binding modes of congeneric series, and interaction conservation.

Splitting my test set by maximum sequence identity to the training data, I showed that DL-based models perform much better close to the training data and worse on more dissimilar proteins–using the entire PoseBusters tests set without subdivision captures only average performance, which is the weakness of time-based splits.

The lesson for practitioners is to consider receptor sequence identity, interaction similarity, ligand chemical similarity, and pocket similarity of protein-complexes of interest and report such metrics on data splits when benchmarking protein-ligand structure prediction methods.
My thesis also makes a methodological contribution.
The usefulness of guidance for adding physical and user biases to diffusion-based structure models is shown.
The GuideDock approach provides a convenient interface for influencing model predictions via force fields, already familiar to practitioners.
I show that any force field term can be used including soft constraints and clash terms.
GuideDock demonstrates that guidance can improve the physical validity of the predictions and allow the user to define a binding site and substructure constraints.
The same principles are applicable to co-folding methods as well.
I have also shown that the DL-based models analysed here have not yet learnt (neither explicitly or implicitly) some of the rules encoded in the force fields.
This suggests that physics and DL-based methods might still be combined successfully.
I demonstrated two ways of doing this: (i) adding an energy minimisation after pose prediction; and (ii) using diffusion guidance with physics-inspired terms.
Both improve the physical plausibility of the generated poses of the methods.
Further ways of combining force fields and diffusion models are easy to think of and should be explored.
Another practical contribution to the field are two new docking test sets.

The first is the PoseBusters test set that includes data both similar to and different from the training data (PDBbind 2020 General), to highlight the current shortcomings of DL-based models and the way they are benchmarked.
The second is the GuideDock test set, which contains pairs of protein-ligand complexes of small molecules that adhere to the same binding pockets on the same protein chain.

The PoseBusters Benchmark set has already been adopted by the scientific community as a test set; the GuideDock set will no doubt be useful for testing template-based and constrained protein-ligand prediction methods.

Finally, I quantified the relationship between the chemical similarity of related ligands and the similarity of their binding poses; this relationship was found to be even stronger for chemical elaborations of smaller ligands.

This finding is of particular relevance to medicinal chemists, as it provides an empirical basis for the substructure constraints used in constrained docking and, more broadly, in fragment-based drug design.

My research has explored and helped improve both DL-based docking and co-folding methods, especially in terms of chemical and physical plausibility.

It has also shown that DL-based protein-ligand docking has not yet reached its potential; however, personally, given the current rate of progress, I believe that DL-based approaches are very likely to become competitive within three years.

I am delighted to have contributed directly to the field by adding new metrics, tools, and benchmark test data sets, providing insights into training data, model performance, different ways to guide diffusion- based models, and ultimately a new guidance model.
